title: Object Modeling & Domain Discovery
description: Techniques for mapping ambiguous problem statements into tangible domain entities, immutable value objects, CRC responsibility cards, and low coupling.

topics.title: Entities vs Value Objects
topics.description: Differentiating between stateful entities with distinct identities and immutable value objects.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: An Entity is an object defined by its unique identity that runs through time (e.g. User ID, Bank Account Number). A Value Object is defined purely by its attributes and has no identity (e.g. Money, DateRange, Address).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Treating everything as an entity creates complex mutable state graphs. Value objects simplify reasoning because they are completely immutable.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: If two objects have identical attributes and are interchangeable, they are Value Objects (e.g. two $10 bills). If they have the same attributes but represent different real-world items, they are Entities (e.g. two twins with different SSNs).

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Entities maintain mutable state protected by invariants. Value objects are initialized in the constructor, have all members marked const, and return new instances upon modification.

sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

comparison.title: Entities vs Value Objects Matrix
rows: class Money { const double amt; const string curr; };

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Address is immutable with value-based equality; User maintains unique identity.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: E-commerce order shipping addresses vs User account entities.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use Value Objects for measurements, coordinates, and currencies. Use Entities for users, orders, and products.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not make Entities immutable if their state naturally evolves over time.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Eliminates concurrency race conditions on value objects; clarifies domain boundaries.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Requires creating new instances when updating value objects.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: DDD Aggregates, Identity vs Attribute comparison.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Giving value objects mutable setter methods.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the difference between entity equality and value object equality?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Entity equality compares unique IDs (e.g. user1.id == user2.id). Value object equality compares all internal attributes (e.g. addr1.street == addr2.street && addr1.zip == addr2.zip).

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement an immutable GeoCoordinate value object validating latitude (-90 to +90) and longitude (-180 to +180).

practice.title: GeoCoordinate Value Object
practice.problemStatement: Implement an immutable GeoCoordinate value object validating latitude (-90 to +90) and longitude (-180 to +180).

referenceCode.code: class GeoCoordinate { public: const double lat, lon; GeoCoordinate(double la, double lo): lat(la), lon(lo) {} };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Entities vs Value Objects is essential for robust Low-Level System Design.

topics.title: CRC Cards & Identifying Responsibilities
topics.description: Class-Responsibility-Collaboration (CRC) technique to identify domain boundaries.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: CRC Cards (Class, Responsibility, Collaborators) are an index-card brainstorming technique to map classes, their obligations, and their helper partners.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Prevents giant God classes by bounding the responsibilities of each class before writing a single line of code.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Every class answers two questions: What do I know? (State) and What do I do? (Behavior).

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Write candidate classes on 3x5 cards. List responsibilities on the left, collaborating classes on the right.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: CRC Structure
callout.text: Class: ParkingLot\nResponsibilities: Manage spot allocation, Calculate total revenue\nCollaborators: ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot, PricingStrategy

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Shows state knowledge and behavioral responsibilities decoupled into collaborators.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: System design interviews for Parking Lot, Elevator, and Ride Sharing.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use during the first 10 minutes of an interview to decompose requirements.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not skip directly to code without bounding responsibilities.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: High cohesion and clear division of labor.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Informal; requires translation to formal UML.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: CRC Brainstorming, Responsibility-Driven Design (RDD).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Assigning 20+ responsibilities to a single class.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the goal of CRC cards in an LLD interview?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: To quickly identify the core noun entities, their verbs (responsibilities), and how they pass messages to collaborating classes.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Model Library, Book, and Member responsibilities.

practice.problemStatement: Model Library, Book, and Member responsibilities.

referenceCode.code: class Book {}; class Member {}; class Library { std::vector<Book> books; };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering CRC Cards & Identifying Responsibilities is essential for robust Low-Level System Design.

topics.title: Domain Invariants & Boundary Design
topics.description: Enforcing business invariants and defining Aggregate Roots in domain modeling.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Domain Invariants are business rules that must ALWAYS hold true throughout the lifetime of an object (e.g. Account balance cannot drop below -$500 overdraft limit).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Guarantees that database records and memory state are never corrupted by invalid concurrent operations.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: An Aggregate Root is the single gateway entity responsible for defending invariants for an entire cluster of child objects (e.g. Order defends OrderItems).

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Constructor verifies invariants upon creation; public mutating methods verify invariants before changing state.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Aggregate Boundary
callout.text: External code must NEVER mutate OrderItem directly. External code asks Order: order.addItem(item), and Order verifies max order limits!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: OrderAggregate strictly guards item count and non-negative pricing invariants.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: E-commerce carts, banking ledger aggregates, flight seat reservation boundaries.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use Aggregate Roots whenever multiple objects have interdependent invariants.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not bypass aggregate roots with direct child setters.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Bulletproof consistency and transactional integrity.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Slight overhead routing calls through the aggregate root.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: DDD Aggregates, Invariant Guards, Preconditions/Postconditions.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Exposing internal mutable collections to callers.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is an Aggregate Root in Low-Level Design?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: An Aggregate Root is a master domain entity that external objects interact with. It encapsulates a cluster of associated objects and strictly defends all internal business invariants.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement a BankAccount that enforces a strict $500 overdraft limit invariant.

practice.title: Bank Account Overdraft Guard
practice.problemStatement: Implement a BankAccount that enforces a strict $500 overdraft limit invariant.

referenceCode.code: class BankAccount { double bal{0}; public: void withdraw(double a) { if(bal - a < -500) throw std::runtime_error('Overdraft'); bal -= a; } };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Domain Invariants & Boundary Design is essential for robust Low-Level System Design.

topics.title: High Cohesion & Low Coupling
topics.description: The twin metrics of software quality: maximizing internal focus and minimizing inter-module dependencies.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Cohesion measures how focused and related the responsibilities of a single module are. Coupling measures how tightly dependent different modules are on each other.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: High Cohesion + Low Coupling = Maintainable, reusable, easily testable architecture.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Goal: High Cohesion (a class does one thing exceptionally well) and Low Coupling (classes communicate through abstract interfaces with minimal direct knowledge).

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Reduce coupling using Dependency Injection and interfaces. Increase cohesion by splitting disparate responsibilities into separate classes.

sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Combines high internal calculation cohesion with low interface payment coupling.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: High-scale distributed systems and enterprise microservices.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Evaluate every new class against cohesion and coupling metrics.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not over-decouple into thousands of 1-line classes (extremes cause complexity).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Maximum maintainability, testability, and parallel team development.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Requires careful interface design up front.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Content coupling, Common coupling, Control coupling, Stamp coupling, Data coupling.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Tight coupling to concrete third-party SDKs.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How do Dependency Injection and Interfaces achieve low coupling?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: They replace concrete type dependencies with abstract contracts, allowing modules to be developed, tested, and replaced without modifying dependent code.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering High Cohesion & Low Coupling is essential for robust Low-Level System Design.
